reviews.content: Professor Higonnet was a great professor! I preferred her lecturer style over that of professor Bryda who teaches part one of the Intro Art History classes (in case you are deciding whether to take part one or two). Although at times she can be a bit slow and stumble on her words, she provides amazing insights into the works of art and her lectures are very engaging. Her exams are also much easier than that of Professor Bryda's. The workload for the class is very minimal and most the readings are not necessary (really depends on your TA). There are two mandatory visits to MET which are really fun and you also have to go on your own for the papers. These MET visits merge class material beautifully with in-person experiences with works of art. Overall this I highly recommend this class and professor Higonnet. However, make sure you choose a good TA, because they will make or break your performance in this class. I received an A in part one of intro to art history but that same quality of work earned mostly Bs with a different TA in this class.

2 2-3 page papers
1 3-4 page paper
Midterm (all IDs)
Final (IDs and one essay)

reviews.content:
Anne Higonnet gets a 10/10 in my book.

She is the spitting image of a classic art historian. She loves all the details, inner workings, historical contexts and it is so fun to watch her get all worked up over things most of us had never noticed!

A previous review called the class boring. That's the kind of basic response I would expect by those who sit in the back row shopping on Zara or scrolling through FB for the 10000000th time that day. In fact, this is a rich class which leaves you with a broad but strong knowledge of the art history you NEED to know in order to understand references and stay relevant.

Sections and Lectures are in perfect synchronicity (better if you have a good TA). Readings were long (sometimes tough) but I literally think about them almost every day. Tests, with the many identification slides and 3 minute short answer sections, were tough and there's no way around them if you don't keep up in class. 

That said, if you're an effective student, there's no reason why you cannot get a stellar grade in this class. What's more, you'll be better for taking it in the long run.
reviews.workload: Weekly reading (25-95 pgs - of which only one reading is imptnt for section), lots of Identification slides to learn (no way around that) and must be able to Viva Vocce about each of them.

reviews.content: Isabella was a wonderful TA for Intro Art History I with Anne Higonnet, and one of the reasons I decided to minor in Art History. I got into her section last minute and I feel so grateful that I did. She's smart, competent, engaging, and made section something I looked forward to every week. That class can be unbearable if you have a bad TA - they grade all your papers/tests, you interact more with them than with Higonnet -  but I lucked out. She cares about the students and is invested in their success throughout the course. I managed to make some of my required trips to the Met with her as well, and her tours were actually interesting (a feat for those trips). She met with me to discuss my papers any time I wanted/needed to, and her comments actually made me think and definitely improved my writing. If you get the chance to have her as your TA, go for it!
reviews.workload: Section is what you make of it, the work is obviously assigned and portioned out by Prof Higonnet, but Isabella does a good job of going over the readings in section. This means if you really don't read them, sometimes you get lucky and can take good notes. But it also means you should come to section having read them if you want to have an engaging conversation.

reviews.content:
I liked Professor Higonnet—her lectures were clear. The workload is fairly manageable—she recommends that you do the reading, but honestly, I did no reading at all and did very well on my midterm. All this class requires in terms of testing is memorization, and if you don't go to lecture, make sure to look up the key works (3 or 4 per class) and write down historical significance/any other important information.  I skipped 1/3 of the lectures, maybe more, and did great, but I did go to discussion section every week.  The essays are not as easy, but if you pay attention to her methods of analyzing the art work, you will do fine—just stand in front of the assigned art for an hour and jot down everything that comes to mind.

Take the testing advice with a grain of salt, because memorization is my forte.  If you aren't good at that, you will have a hard time on the midterm and final.

reviews.content: I think Professor Waters did a great job. I feel like he made sure to keep the class engaging even while going through quite a lot of material since the class is more of a general overview of architecture and spans many centuries and regions. His courseworks was extremely organized, he would post the slides prior to class and always had study guides with buildings we would be quizzed on and a list of important categories. As a STEM major I would say it doesn't take much to do well in this class as long as you just do the work and show up to class as he doesn't post recordings of the class until reading week. Would highly recommend this class it's fun, interesting, and you decide how much effort you want to put into the class.
reviews.workload: There are 3 quizzes that are all take home and 1 in person final that was around 2 hours. He allows a double sided cheat sheet on the final which helps with dates and names of buildings along with a bullet point or two for more detail. There were optional readings for class that I never looked at and I don't feel like I missed out. The only thing that was actually do weekly was for the discussion section and most of the readings were pretty short. There were also 3 short essays that mostly focused on the writing itself rather than the buildings it was talking about. The one other assignment we had was a building analysis which was around 6 pages that I felt was similar to writing a lab report about a building.

reviews.content:
This review is for the intro to the history of architecture with professor waters, a real king. 
Let me start off by saying I took this course as a freshman in the fall, started taking it at the end of add/drop period, and ended with an A. I recommend this course to everyone that is looking for something that isn't too much of a heavy workload, looking for an easy A, and isn't bored with learning about the architecture and cultural atmosphere in Greece, China, Japan, Rome, New York, UK, etc. There is a discussion section for the course but that was very manageable you just go through a previous text you analyzed for hw and don't even need to speak too much. 
The way professor waters teaches is lecture-based with a few guest lecturers. I took this in the fall of 2020 so this was all via zoom yet professor waters makes the lecture actually interesting and engaging so that you don't really lose focus. You learn stuff like what type of column is used in what architectural style and why the architect decided to use and create it.  It was genuinely nice to learn and definitely gave me a greater appreciation for a lot of beautiful buildings. You also learn about the culture surrounding the time period when a structure was made ignorer to fully understand why and how it was created and what purpose it serves. I really like how he does this because you learn so much about these famous cities that you didn't know before.
Waters smiles a lot when he's talking about something he is particularly excited about, which is really refreshing to see a professor who actually really understands what he's teaching enough to make small little jokes you can catch if you pay attention. He is also super understanding if people email him with concerns about a quiz or deadline he changes it so that his students don't need to worry. The TAs are also all really nice and helpful if you have questions
Literally, just pay attention in class and take notes. The way I did it is typing notes all onto one google doc and that way I could command f things for quizzes or papers or the final. That's really all you have to do in order to get an A. So definitely take this course even if you aren't majoring in architecture. I'm a CS major and I'm so glad I took it.

Professor Waters was excellent. He's new to Columbia and possibly new to teaching in general, however I have never seen a teacher so well prepared yet capable of going off script. Every class he gave us a sheet containing all the important terms and buildings. He also build the class around five themes that he managed to flesh out and make clear. 
He also managed to make the discussion sections more substantial than going over what was said in lecture. Each one added to the overall themes and often included short field trips. 
I see a gold nugget in the making.
reviews.workload: Very reasonable. The readings generally were short articles or passages from architectural books. We wrote five short (500 word) response papers and had four building recognition quizzes. The biggest projects were the final and a visual analysis paper that required you to go to a building and see it, but even this was only five pages and he gave us a month and a half to do it. Nothing felt tedious.

reviews.content:
Professor Kay does not a good professor. She is not enthusiastic in class, is a boring lecturer, does not explain concepts well, creates bad exams (she is not clear in her questions what she wants the answer to be), and does not accommodate students with disabilities well (for quizzes, if they are unable to come to class early to get their extra time, she has them sit in the hallway and miss part of the lecture to finish the quiz). 

This being said, Stars, Galaxies and Cosmology is a very easy class to pass. She drops the lowest homework and quiz grade, the quizzes are open notes, and you get one page of notes for the midterm, and two pages for the final. She also offers an extra credit assignment (paper 3-4 pages long about an exhibit at the Natural History Museum or a book on astronomy). And, because so many people take this class to fulfill the quantitative reasoning or lab science requirement, and are just looking for a pass, the curve is HUGE. She also posts the power points from class online beforehand, so you only need to take notes on any extra or clarifying information she says in class (but she does not always post them ahead of time, and not all the information from the in-class powerpoint is the a same as the one on courseworks).

But if you're actually looking to understand the concepts, you need to put in a lot of extra work on your own, go to office hours, and I would recommend taking the lab. If I had not been in lab for this class, I would not have understood many of the concepts as well as I did. Also, a physics or math background (which I have) is extremely helpful, as she does not go over how to use the equations in class. If you want a sample math problem done out, you need to go to office hours.
reviews.workload:

Lowest homework and quiz get dropped, and you are allowed one page of notes for the midterm, and two pages for the final.

reviews.content:
Are you a SEAS junior or senior with some time on your hands and want 2 easy A's (possibly A+'s) to boost your GPA? Are you interested in Astro? Then these classes are the classes for you- minimum amount of work for maximum grade return.

Here's some back story- I found myself starting 2nd semester junior year just having gotten the lowest GPA I had ever had. I had literally hit rock bottom. I needed some A's to neutralize the bad grades I got and my major courses weren't helping, so I decided to take this class and what a great decision it was. Yes, they fulfill literally no requirement, but they also factor into your GPA, and 6 credits of A isn't insignificant.

As a SEAS junior or senior in an intro Barnard science class, let's just say it couldn't possibly get more stacked. I literally never went to class except for exams and to hand in homework. Just printing and reading the powerpoints posted online for maybe 10-15 minutes a week is more than enough to learn all the material in this class. The homework is so easy that it becomes almost enjoyable to do them. As a SEAS junior, I'm used to looking at a pset and thinking, Crap, I have no idea how to do this. As a result, just being able to understand all the work at first glance makes me feel accomplished since I'm so used to getting completely pwned by work. Quizzes are also easy as pie. Never study for them- just print the powerpoints and use them in the open book quiz. The questions are real straightforward, just plug and chug. I found myself consistently the first to finish. Midterms and the final, while not open book, are similarly easy and require a minimum of studying. Heck, you even get something you will never ever hear about in a SEAS course- extra credit. In the spring it was a book report- something I hadn't seen since elementary school.

Just a few examples of how easy the course is- the textbook (which is online by the way), literally teaches you ROYGBIV. And in the powerpoints, Kay actually reassures you that there isn't much math and to not panic when logarithms are introduced, as if those would make someone bat an eye, much less drop the class (oh wait...)

In the end, I aced nearly everything and got an easy 6 credits of A with almost no work at all. And to boot, I also got an awesome boost in self esteem and confidence from being easily at the top of the class- something that hasn't happened since high school.

reviews.content:
Do not take this class. If youâ€™re anything like me, youâ€™re a non â€“math or -science major looking for the path of least resistance to fulfilling your science requirements. This is not that path. 

To be fair, this class is some of the things youâ€™re looking for: absolutely no attendance is required save the midterm, final, and quiz days, nor would it benefit you â€“ of all the bored people with glazed eyes that fill the lecture hall, Professor Kay is by far the most bored of all, her eyes glazier than any. Kay stands up front, reads her Power Points verbatim, and then posts them at the end of class for everyone to download â€“ I can genuinely say I sat through not one full lecture. And it wasnâ€™t for want of trying; each month Iâ€™d recommit to attending class and being participatory, and each time that I tried I fled the lecture near the halfway point, re-outraged and re-in-disbelief that all the professor does is quite literally stand at the front of the room and read her bloody slides. Frankly, I am qualified to teach this course. 

And please donâ€™t misunderstand me: itâ€™s not like I wasnâ€™t interested, and Iâ€™m not allergic to science or anything. Rather, the class is structured in such a way as to wholly eradicate anyoneâ€™s interest in the cosmos; itâ€™s an inferno for even the slightest hint of interest or passion you might casually harbor for the subject of stars and the like. The six homework assignments and five quizzes ensure that something is due every week, and the vast majority of the work is math based. The math is by no means difficult, but the concepts necessary to understand the correct application of the given formulas is also never taught, making the process of figuring out what to do with which pieces of information a real bitch. Whatâ€™s worse, the grading system is really just one big fat curve that doesnâ€™t get applied till after the final, so basically you spend the entire semester getting 16/25 on this quiz and 14/20 on that homework, and stressing frantically about how this stupid class is going to ruin your GPA and wondering whether or not you should cover it up and if itâ€™s even too late to do that, and then, lo and behold, two and half weeks after the semester ends SSOL tells you *Your grade has recently been submitted here* and you click the hyperlinked â€˜hereâ€™ and thereâ€™s a decent grade sitting in the box next to Stars, Galaxies, and the Cosmos. 

Please donâ€™t get me wrong â€“ Iâ€™m not an embittered student seething about a poor grade, or an angry Gender Studies major vexed I had to sit through a class where someone made us use the â€˜Cosâ€™ button on a calculator. I got an A, and I was very interested in the material going in. That being said, I spent the entire semester under the pretty-understandable delusion that I was getting a C, I resented every single homework assignment that asked us to apply formulas to complicated concepts that were absolutely never discussed in class, and I reviled the quizzes that seemed a deliberate attempt to conceal what form the answer should be in â€“ often times I would get 7 points off a 20 point quiz for giving a numerical answer when a verbal one was required, and I was far from the only one. Ultimately, I went through the entire semester feeling ignorant of and combative with the material, and the fact that I ended up on the good side of the curve only deepens the farce, indicating how poorly everyone else must have done. 

In a word, I can only say that this class seems wholly and perfectly designed to suffocate any interest you may have in astronomy, and to demoralize and discourage those of us silly enough to hope we might enjoy an introductory course in a subject unrelated to our major.

reviews.content:
Maybe, in a couple of years' time, these two instructors will be decent lecturers. For the present, they're just plain bad (consider the fact that Mowshowitz sat in on two of our lectures). Perez-Cheeks is marginally better than Lim, but I may be biased because I found her material more interesting. 

The first couple of lectures were insanely rushed because Lim assumed we'd learned it all in intro bio. Like the previous review said, whenever Lim didn't like the Clicker responses, she'd tell us that we needed to review the material. The fact is, we never actually LEARNED that stuff in intro bio (at least not in such depth), which only covered the very basics. My main frustration was that with all the time she spent talking about how we needed to review intro bio material, she could have just taught the material to us.

Even when she did slow down to re-cap the more confusing concepts, it wasn't that helpful because she couldn't explain it any differently from the book. I'm fine with textbook lecturers if the textbook is any good, but our textbook was terrible, so Lim's offhanded responses ("Well, this was in your book, so take a look at that") were hardly reassuring. She also liked to work out problems on the overhead, but her explanation of the process sounded like something regurgitated and didn't really give us time to absorb the information. 

Perez-Cheeks was at least a clearer lecturer, but she lectured heavily from an unassigned textbook (which was kept on reserve). With such a heavy emphasis on prokaryotic genetics, I wish they'd assigned us a more comprehensive textbook. 

I think my main issue was that it was so obvious neither of them really wanted to teach this class. For the most part, they slavishly followed the textbook's explanations without stopping to consider whether the textbook was all that good at explaining the concepts. At the beginning of the semester, they told us that they would prefer it if we emailed the TAs instead of them because it'd be too time-consuming to respond to so many emails. On top of that, they didn't hold office hours because neither of them worked on the Morningside campus (the logic being that in the past, no one had bothered going to office hours when they were held at the medical campus... So why couldn't they have reserved a room on campus for an hour or two before each class?). This meant that if we wanted to ask them questions directly, we had to cram them into the few minutes before and after class. I'm sure a lot of people just resorted to emailing them anyway, but I was floored by how eager they were to distance themselves from the class.
reviews.workload: Medium for a bio class for undergrads. Weekly problem sets (mostly from the textbook, which makes it easy if you have the solutions manual, but they take off points if it's obvious you just copied the answers). Five 10-minute, MC quizzes throughout the semester. Two midterms and one final. Participation is taken via the clicker (so you can't miss too many classes).

reviews.content:
The semester started out pretty inauspiciously, with Lim rushing through the lectures absurdly fast, making obvious errors/getting somewhat offended when people pointed them out, and spending over 15 minutes fiddling with the stupid iClicker software. This software was particularly useless during these first few lectures when, even when she saw that less than half of the class got the right answers to the clicker questions, she dismissed the class's lack of understanding telling us "You should have learned this in intro bio" and that we should "go review it on our own time." Eventually she got the picture and slowed down for a few lectures, unfortunately to a snail-like pace that left many asleep. 

Thankfully, by a month or two into the semester she figured out a decent pace and started getting her act together. There were still a few topics that seemed very rushed, though, and more than once I had to go home and reread the lecture notes before I understood a lick of what she was talking about. 

I preferred Perez-Cheeks as a professor, though I wasn't crazy about the actual material she taught.  The class discussed more prokaryotic genetics than I particularly cared for. This was especially problematic due to the fact that our textbook was primarily eukaryote focused, leaving Perez-Cheeks to assign homework out of a textbook nobody owned (she thought she rectified this by keeping the secondary text on reserve, a slightly laughable idea since it was two copies for about 80 students.). Not that the book was particularly useful for the material it actually did cover. In fact, I found myself referencing Becker (World of the Cell, from Mowshowitz bio) more than our textbook. 

There were some times when the class felt exceedingly disorganized, which had me feeling nostalgic for Mowshowitz's wonderfully choreographed teaching. The material was often presented in a strange order, material awkwardly switching between eukaryotic and prokaryotic or being taught almost piecemeal.

But all in all, the class ended up being decent, despite its flaws. They definitely weren't the best professors, but they weren't the worst by any means, and were generally nice people. It was even somewhat interesting at times, and I could stay awake through it most of the time.

One CUMULATIVE final.

Engaging professor, but Yin should not be teaching. As sweet and good-intentioned as she is, she's a horrible teacher. Aviv is interesting, though goes really fast. If you miss a beat, you won't get the rest of the lecture. The subject material itself isn't extremely captivating, at least not the way it is taught. The textbook was much more interesting, at least to me. If you're the kind of person who needs to get a lot of details to work into the general, the book would be useful.

Professor Aviv, I know you're reading this so PLEASE put up some sort of powerpoint BEFORE class. As much as you are opposed to this, it'll be a huge help those who are a bit slower at picking up material. And slow down during the Lambda phage lessons. You went way too fast there and did not break up the different stages distinctively enough.
reviews.workload: 3-4 midterms + final. No homework, but you must keep up or you'll be completely lost.

reviews.content: Aviv is an energetic professor that seems to care about his class and his field of work.  That is until he had a first time grad student (Yin Mei Lim) teach a little over half the course (but more (now professor) Yin Mei Lim).  His office hours are in the morning and at the medical campus, thus it is quite inaccessible (why can't he just have them on the college campus?).  His lectures are quite interesting, and you must study them religiously since the exams are solely based on his lectures and some extra material such as a research paper or a wiki article (on lambda phage).  Now, with Lim: she tried at first to write on the black board, to utter failure.  Then she tried writing on a projector, to utter failure.  Finally, she resorted to doing her lectures via powerpoint, like what Aviv does.  But, her lectures were much more tepid, boring, and straight from the textbook.  Also, you must go over all your exams (including your final), because the TAs (I've heard) will make some mistakes on grading.
reviews.workload: Readings from a good textbook (but only needed as supplement... wiki and google works much better, and they don't cost over $$$), an research article or two, and weekly problems either made by the profs or from the textbook.

reviews.content: AVOID at ALL costs! I have always loved biology, that is until I had Morton. Among all the biology teachers/professors I have had in high school and college, he is by far the worst! He is very disorganized, so it is extremely difficult to follow his lectures. Also, his lectures are incredibly boring, it's really hard not to space out at times. Morton pretends to be nice and helpful sometimes, but i don't think he cares a lot about his students at all. If you absolutely have to take this course, then take it with Mansfield! she teaches it in the Spring.
reviews.workload: fairly heavy, 2 midterms, 1 final. all pretty hard.

reviews.content:
She is boring. The class material is boring, but she is even more boring.

The grading for labs is barely explain and when you go to the instructors, they confuse you even more. People I know get low grades and P/D/F the next semester, if take it at all.

Professor Heller is a nice person, but boy is she unhelpful! When you come into her lecture, you see a bunch of slides and her talking on the background. Well, if you hadn't read the book the night before, she will make no sense. So read the book - then at least you will understand what on this planet Professor Heller is talking about!
reviews.workload: No homeworks, two midterms, one final. The book is boring, but you will have to read it once to get a B or B+.

The textbook is Anatomy and Physiology for Dummies.  FOR DUMMIES?  
I am ashamed that the Bio department allows this non-textbook to be 
used.

reviews.content: Definitely A LOT of memorization. I don't think she's as bad as some of the previous reviews mentioned, but she can go way too into depth about some topics and then rush through the rest of her PowerPoint. Thankfully she posts the slides and her tests are pretty straightforward, only consisting of concepts and definitions she taught during lectures. One thing I appreciate about Prof. Wooley is her passion for what she teaches; it makes the lectures a lot more interesting to listen to. That being said, only take this class if you're genuinely interested in animal behavior. Otherwise, it's just painful memorization.

Okay... I took this class thinking the reviews must be outdated or something. Certainly, she can't be *that* bad... but now I know I would not have taken this class if I knew what I knew now. It is not hard, per se, but my only goal is to pass so whatever.
Anyway, Dr. Woolley is very passionate about the material, but I do not actually learn much from lectures. They are interesting, but you have to read the relevant scientific studies if you want good grades on exams. I only attend lectures because she produces verbal sound effects for every animal and my girlfriend thinks it's hilarious.
She is very strict about deadlines and extensions.
She's so sweet. Great for a first Upper Level Bio class, or if you want to know cool facts, or have a science but lighter load.

Professor Pischedda is a FANTASTIC professor. She is hilarious, kind, and genuinely wants her students to succeed and actually learn the material, not just memorize a bunch of facts. I took this course during Spring 2021 in the immersive format, so it definitely was different than in past years, especially because there were no exams. However, I feel like I learned more in this class without exams because instead, we had to write answers to "critical thinking" questions and actually take the time to apply what we learned. Take this class!

After a year of waiting to write this review, I have gone back to my notes which I have kept regarding my interactions with Sarah Woolley, solely for the sake of moral justice. This is a cautionary tale for those who are considering taking her class, highlighting reactions of Professor Woolley to the unexpected situation of one of her students having a concussion a few days before the first exam of the semester. Throughout my experience she has proven to lacks basic communication and social skills, actively go against the values of the profession of teaching, and shown more empathy towards the birds she researches than her actual human students. I have never had such a bad experience with not only a teacher but any other human being that I inhabit this planet with until taking Professor Woolley's class. If you are reading this review, I would suggest do not take her class, and also do anything in your power to not have to interact with this lady until you graduate.

All of this started when she refused to write me a make up exam after I was abruptly hospitalized for a concussion the weekend before the actual date, and with the doctors medical suggestion found out that I should not take the official make up but instead be administered an exam a week later. She did not reply to my emails regarding the matter, and was extremely pissed off that she had to write another make up. When my advisor interfered and she actually had to write it, she omitted information like points appointed for each question that every other student had on their exam. She was unresponsive to all of my emails throughout the whole recovery process of 10 weeks, except when she asked for my advisors email because she believed my frustration with not being able to get access to slides for the lectures I missed with a doctors suggestion was a violation of conduct due to its not so friendly tone. She literally refused to open her door during office hours before my make up while I knocked and emailed outside her door, and instead followed through with an email cancelling her office hours 15 minutes in while she was literally inside of her office and I was at the door. I managed to schedule another office hour with the interference of my advisor once again, which she cancelled the last minute (and her TA straight up did not show up to) and therefore managed to not see me before administering this make up exam. When I took the exam two weeks after my concussion without information about the three lectures I missed and got a 45, I did manage to get into an office hour with her to go over my mistakes in which she had the decency to make comments like "I do not have to see you" and call me out for my pronunciation of certain words. When I questioned her motives in correcting my pronunciation she responded with "I thought you wanted me to help you and that is why you are here", insinuating that I was trying to get points off of her I did not deserve with this office hour and not actually learn. Not only that, but she took it upon herself to correct my English as a second language pronunciation when a week prior she was literally refusing to open her door to go over questions I had about the lecture material during her office hours.

This professor will treat you like dirt under her shoe until she makes you cry and not bat an eye, smirking at your face in victory while you explain to her how she is bullying you and abusing her position of power when she is correcting your pronunciation and calling that  "helping you". She refuses to see, recognize or appreciate effort of any kind and is a literal adult bully that will go out of her way to make you feel insecure, incapable and inferior. I have never ever expected to interact with such an immoral professor, and am honestly still disappointed to this day that Columbia would hold such a despicable professor in their psychology department for the sake of her research. Do not take her class if you do not want to get bullied and triple the huge stress you are already experiencing in this institution.
reviews.workload: Learn it yourself from the book and spare yourself spending your tuition on this course because she is definitely not going to answer your questions or even care if you are registering the material.

reviews.content: This class was so mid. He is so mid. He reads off the slides the entire time and is just kind of.. not that into it. His tests are CRAZY. You would think to yourself.. some MCQ! Oh ok! Mans wants to go off script and do some open response- that's actually totally fine! But his grading is _not_ totally fine. It's all over the place. Like giving 3/5 points for no reason and giving other people 5/5 for the same answer?? You have to go to office hours and talk everything out... before the test, after the test, it's a nightmare. He also won't curve the grade. It's the oddest thing. Maybe he was just going through something last spring. Either way - I would avoid if you could.
reviews.workload: There are these problem sets too - not bad like group-based, and you have a week to do them. Then these easy mcq online quizzes every week based on the lectures. The 3 tests are off-the-chart insane, and he just doesn't really take feedback well. This class has a lot of potential but he just doesn't really do the subject justice in my opinion. Good luck!!

reviews.content: Professor Balaban is super nice and passionate about physiology. The course is heavily muscle and neuro heavy, as that's what Professors Glendinning (other prof who teaches the class) and Balaban study. Professor Balaban is generally really accommodating and a decent lecturer. Physiology is inevitably dense and a lot of memorization, but Balaban does try to make it interesting. It's his first time teaching the course so he is definitely still finding his feet and it was a bit disorganized. The tests can also be fairly confusing. I think as he teaches it more it'll run a little more smoothly in terms of pacing. He does make his lectures as entertaining as possible and is clear about what you need to know
reviews.workload:
2 midterms, last midterm during finals 
3 quizzes (only 3 questions) on papers --> maybe 20 mins each 
3 psets (as a group project) --> 3-4 hours each 
readings for lecture --> 1 hour each

reviews.content:
I had Prof. Glendinning for physiology this semester, and I loved the class and his teaching style!  He sets very clear, reasonable expectations for students, so you never have to wonder what will or won't be on the exams.  The class is very process-based (it's physiology, obviously) and it's great for people interested in real world applications of bio, like medicine or sports.  I also love that he includes research articles in the coursework.  His lectures are very clear and organized.  The textbook isn't necessary, but it's great to use as a reference if something, in particular, has been difficult to understand.  Prof. Glendinning also asks lots of questions during class, so those who do the readings or preview the slides can feel rewarded for their efforts when they know the answers.  He brought a real brain to class one time, so be prepared for that!  
Overall a great class, 10/10 would recommend!
reviews.workload: a couple exams, some quizes on the research articles, some group problem sets, regular readings are assigned

BIOL BC1503.courseName: Intro Lab to Cellular and Molecule Biology

reviews.content:
I too walked in the first day of lab panicking from what legend says about Wanda. I shook as she hovered over me watching me micropipette and sweat whenever she asked me a question. After some time i started to understand her. She just has a really dry sense of humor and most people take it as her being mean. She means business but also really wants you to understand what the experiment is. She breaks down the procedure for lab to make it really easy to understand. She repeats herself constantly and makes sure you know what you are doing. She tells you exactly what she wants in her lab reports so while she goes on an hour rant about her expectations DON'T ZONE OUT! She really tells you exactly what to write so pay attention! 
So all in all she is really scary but she's also really funny once you break down that barrier of intimidation.  Also always ask your TAs for help they are amazing.
reviews.workload: 2 lab reports, final midterm, weekly quizzes

reviews.content:
Dr. Mowshowitz is a terrible teacher.  While her lectures are occasionally interesting, she is nasty to her students.  I always thought it was the duty of a professor to 'set their students up for success'.  Dr. M sets you up for failure.  

I didn't do as well as I wanted on the first exam of the semester.  I went to her an explained my study habits and asked for some advice on how to improve.  She essentially went through my exam and told me that I should have known the things I got wrong and offered no advice.  

I did all the homework problems, and I did them in groups and alone.  Normally, one would assume that the homework would provide practice for the exam, or at least show you the importance of topics (for example, more problems on one subject would mean it was more important).  This wasn't the case.  The one problem made of terms she only mentioned once (I searched through the lecture notes) was a quarter of the exam.  

I sought out tutors for the finals.  The ones she had listed for the most part didn't know the material.  When I mentioned what I was feeling in the course (that the material given to me had little baring on the exam), they all understood and said that most of their students felt the same.

I think this course can be summed up by a conversation I took part in earlier in the semester.  I was talking with two students, one that didn't really put in much effort, and another that went to both lectures, read all the lecture notes, took notes on the lecture notes, and did all the problems twice.  The one who didn't put in much effort did above the mean, and the one who put in an insane amount of work got well below the mean.  This course teaches steps a and b, but tests on step m in the made up language that Mowshowitz speaks.

For anyone who sits there and tries to say that the people complaining are just lazy and mean spirited, you happened to be the small percentage of people who speaks Dr. M's language, a skill that has nothing to do with biology, being a scientist, or being a doctor.  I hate that this woman thinks that she has the sole duty of determining who is qualified for med school, something I don't even want to do, and decides that she must be the gate keeper.
reviews.workload: irrelevent.  the problems she gives has nothing to do with how well you will do, don't provide accurate practice or ability to judge your knowledge.

reviews.content: Wanda Knauss has a really bad reputation but is no where near as bad as people seem to think. I've had her for two semesters now and am glad for it. She's extremely intelligent and is always willing to help. However, she doesn't spoon feed you answers. Instead she asks questions in a way that lead you to the correct answer. In other words, you actually have to use your brain. She's also not an easy grader and can be picky, but I learned a lot from her. Frankly, too many people seem keen on blaming her for their own mistakes. A lot of the corrections she makes make sense. If you want to do well in her class just pay attention, actually learn the material, and be ready to think.
reviews.workload: Moderate: two lab reports, one midterm, and a final.

reviews.content: Wanda is a mean-spirited person and will ruin your grade.  By all means avoid her lab section.  She made me miserable all semester and Dr. Goldstein,who runs the labs did nothing about it, even after I went to her for consolation.
reviews.workload: She made writing lab reports extremely unpleasant.  Her instructions were always vage and and was a completely unfair grader.  As a result, you'll work harder and do worse than if you were in another section.

reviews.content:
If you get Nora for your lab instructor, you should thank your lucky stars. This was her first semester, and I think she did an amazing job. She's really knowledgeable about the material and can help you out with any questions you have during lab, but she keeps her opening lecture concise, which is helpful. 

She's also an extremely fair grader. She makes lots of useful comments and corrections on the homework, but doesn't necessarily take off points for every little mistake. 

The best part about Nora is that she's extremely friendly and approachable (unlike some of the other lab instructors). Definitely take her section if you can.
reviews.workload: Not too bad. Lab worksheets, a pre-lab quiz and an outline of the procedure for each class as well as two formal lab reports. One midterm (not a practical, like in the lab for Hertz's class) and one final, both reasonable if you study.

BIOL BC1502.courseName: Introduction to Cell and Molecular Biology

reviews.content: Explains concepts well and lecture slides are very detailed on what is covered on test. Engaging speaker although feels like content is read off slides but the slides posted are enough to be able to study for tests. Test questions aren't too hard if you study the study guide material (also comprehensive of what will be on test) and curves to average of 85.
reviews.workload: 3 midterms and cumulative final each worth 18.75%. weekly hw is 15% where it is based off completion and can hand in up to 2 late and randomly taken attendance by activity is 10%.

reviews.content: There was a lot of content -- moved through about a chapter of the textbook a week but it was pretty dense. Dr. Shah is a wonderful professor though and always wanting to help. She answers in class questions really well and communicates the information in a digestible way. I definitely recommend taking her section of this class, no negative notes.
reviews.workload: One page paper (easy), 3 midterms, weekly HW quizzes (easy), one cumulative final. Midterms curved to an 85% average.

reviews.content: Okay. You are not going to die in this class; ignore the other review. However, it is hard. If you aren't taking this for your major or premed, don't take it. Find an easier class. She posts her slides now, so there's that. Overall, she's really sweet and funny and really tries to help us understand the content more than just memorize. However, there is WAY too much content. (Not the professor's fault, it's the course's fault.) It's almost impossible to know everything. The tests are not just about memorization but about being able to apply what you know to other situations, which demands a deeper understanding, which is almost impossible with so much content. For premeds and science majors, this is a class you have to take, so just get through it. But be prepared that it is hard. It isn't impossible to get a good grade. But it's hard.
reviews.workload: There is a project where you have to write a one-page paper, super easy. three midterms, one cumulative final. hours upon hours of studying for those. Homework is just readings with super easy quizzes to check for reading being done that take thirty seconds and you can look them up.

reviews.content: Harder than the first semester bio. Much more abstract concepts and way more terms. Pay attention in lecture and I found that the best way to study was to explain concepts out loud to the TA's and they help clarify any confusions from there. Content is easier for those who have taken some form of biology in the past (ex. I got an A and had a phenomenal AP Bio teacher in high school).
reviews.workload: The quizzes are hard, you do best when you collaborate. Don't assume the content is easy and that you'll do fine, you likely won't. The wording is very specific in them, concepts are mentioned for a reason. Pay super close attention in lectures because Snow might mention something only once and it will be on the quiz. His exams are much better. They're still crazy hard, but the questions are easier than on the quiz and the concepts they ask about are pretty reasonable. The quizzes were 12.5% of the grade and the average was curved to a 97 (yeah, I know). Each exam was 22.5% and then there was a attendance and SimBio hw grade which were both easy A's. I personally got A's on all three exams, but the average was typically a 75%. The best way to study is to start early and attend office hours even if you don't have specific questions.

reviews.content: He’s not a great teacher but tests are very very fair. Memorization based and he will try to trick you but LEAGUES better than Shah was (dropped it with Shah last semester and now am getting an A in Snow’s…so that should tell you something )
reviews.workload: Reasonable

reviews.content: I honestly didn’t know what to expect what I signed up for this course. Overall, I would say start attending office hours early. Professor Morton, I found, was an extremely agreeable professor who really searched to try to test your knowledge. When I was doing exams, as long as you provided information to show you studied, he’d be very lenient with grading. He also was very good with returning grades on time. He’s just really nice!
reviews.workload:
I’d just say that because there’s only two midterms and they’re very spaced out, the content can feel overwhelming. You really need to lock in on the material before exams, and I mean begin studying and reviewing the processes WHILE they’re being taught. That was my flaw at least. His exams always have definition questions, and short-answer problems. Be prepared to really explain yourself for the definitions, go into detail on what you know for each. 

Workload: 2 midterms (Each weighed 25%), 3 Problem sets (15%), and one final (35%).

reviews.content: she is one of the best and kindest professors i have had in my educational path. she is a good lecturer and her exams and grading is fair. she is passionate about the material and her research. if you do the work you will succeed in this class.
reviews.workload: a decent amount of work. officer hours is needed

reviews.content: Going into this class and reading CULPA reviews made me nervous to say the least. I can't say Prof Morton was always 1000% clear with his teaching. he was also sometimes quite dry, and his problem sets and tests were difficult. that being said -- professor morton was one of the kindest professors i have ever seen who was so incredibly dedicated to helping his students succesd. his tests had much memorization but were relatively straight forward, and he gave a ton of partial credit if you showed yiu studied and knew something. would 10000000% take him over mansfield if you have the choice
reviews.workload:
2 midterms and a final
for the Mendelian half, a problem set due every other week that was pretty involved (start early)

reviews.content: Taking this class with Professor Mansfield encouraged me to pursue the full Biology major, rather than just the minor. The content of her class inspired me to keep taking biology electives, particularly her Topics in Genetics class the following semester. Her lectures were clear, and she is an extremely reasonable person in terms of her grading, workloads, and due dates. If you enjoy this class, I also highly recommend taking her Topics class when she offers it! As someone interested in genetics, this was an amazing introduction and opportunity to delve deeper into some of the most interesting topics from the first semester. A large part of the content in this course was going over lab techniques, which proved especially helpful the following summer when I worked in a genetics lab! The class also includes a journal club aspect, with weekly assigned current papers in genetics, and each person presents one paper for the class.
reviews.workload:
Molecular and Mendelian Genetics: 2 midterms, and midterm 3 + final combined where we had the entire finals period to complete the third midterm and a short cumulative final. These could be challenging, but the content that was assessed was always from the lectures/slides. (kind of) weekly PSETs that were more challenging than the exams but were great practice. She occasionally uploaded them late, in which cases she was very accommodating in offering extensions. Each PSET took about 1-2 hours a week 
Topics: 2 midterms, one was during the finals period. Finals also included a final journal club paper that we were given ahead of time, encouraged to work together on, and asked questions about in the final. Again, very reasonable in terms of the content that was assessed. Weekly journal club paper + posting a question about it, usually took about 1-2 hours if you want to deeply read and understand the paper. You are assigned one paper to present in full (30 min presentation), plus leading the journal club discussion afterwards. This took the most time during the semester, although she encouraged you to meet with her beforehand and she will go over the paper with you and basically share what parts she's expecting you to present.

reviews.content: take it with someone else, she is really nice but tbh i did not like her teaching. the tests were really really hard. the grading was very unclear. i ended with a c i think even though i would study so much and had her content slides memorized, it just wasn't enough. the problem sets are a little challenging but do impact ur grade. this course just felt insanely hard for a 2000 level class. idk id take with someone else tbh
reviews.workload: problem sets, 2 midterms, 1 final (worth 35% of the grade, 2 parts so most of it focused on the last third of the content, but still need to study everything), the average exam grades were in the 70s, she does curve but it was really unclear how

reviews.content: Super clear professor in what exams will be, definitely difficult in terms of content but that is just biochem. If you put in the work for studying there are no surprises on her exams. Everything else is basically graded on completion and you also have the option to do test corrections which was super helpful.
reviews.workload: 3 exams, lecture worksheets graded on completion, final literature review. She offers test corrections for points back on the exam which truly saved my grade. Also is super chill with deadlines.

reviews.content:
Seems like a nice person (she always brings us candy on exam days) but is by far the worst and most incompetent lecturer I've had during my time here. Frequently cancels office hours/problem sessions and this makes her inaccessible, it's impossible to get some 1-on-1 time with her, and she once didn't even show up to a session because she "totally forgot." During lecture she often forgets what she says, or backtracks and confuses the class (I'd actually prefer she read off the slide because then it'd be easier to follow). I also think it's pretty hypocritical of her to expect us to remember and regurgitate months' worth of information when she can't even get through a single lecture correctly WITH notes. She assigns problem sets due every two weeks that are a hassle to get through, and doesn't even grade them. I don't think she grades anything that gets handed to her in its entirety because I've definitely received exams where the grader's handwriting changes halfway. You'd think she would hand things back quicker if she had a bunch of Chem department drones doing her work for her.

I don't recommend taking biochem with her. Take it at Columbia instead.
reviews.workload: 3 exams that she doesn't even entirely grade (I hear some poor Chem department TAs or graders get conscripted to do a lot of her dirty work); problem set every 2 weeks that is unnecessarily long and isn't even graded.

reviews.content:
Professor Sever is probably the most incompetent professor I have ever encountered here at Barnard and Columbia.  First off, she is extremely unreliable in handing back assignments and tests.  I have to say, she was quite good with the first test, but we have not gotten back our second test and it has been over two weeks.  Furthermore, we haven't gotten back our problem sets from several weeks ago; she also is not timely in posting solutions to the problem sets on Courseworks.  Furthermore, the problem sets are difficult and students do put in effort into them, but she doesn't even to bother to check them; the few problem sets that we have gotten back have no markings on them whatsoever.  

She is also a very poor lecturer, simply reading off the slides that she posts.  She also frequently says wrong information in class, someone will point it out, and then she'll get confused and flustered and ultimately confuse the rest of the class.  She is not responsible; one time, she missed a recitation section and we all waited for her to show up for twenty minutes!  It's super disappointing to be in a challenging class and to not have a professor who is responsible and reliable.  Professor Sever has really confirmed the inadequacies of the Chemistry Department at Barnard.
reviews.workload: Three tests and a final; first test was difficult and rather long, second test not as long and not as difficult, but required a TON of writing, third test coming up soon.  Final is cumulative.  Problem sets every two weeks, not graded, just 'spot-checked' by Professor Sever.

reviews.content: This guy is a gem. The best. Take any class that is offered with him.
reviews.workload: He is really understanding and a great prof. He gets to know his students and is very passionate about what he is teaching. Highly recommend! The workload is appropriate for lab. The pre-lab quiz can be a tad difficult, but it's doable if you study the pre-lab materials. Then there's a group lab assignment, and you're graded on weekly questions from the lab.

reviews.content: Great Professor! Talked us through each lab is great detail and helps you out with anything. He is super clear about lab report expectations. One of the easiest labs to take if you are looking for an upper level lab. Cannot recommend him enough.
reviews.workload: 2 Lab reports (1 being for the final project), Pre-lab quizzes every week, Lab report questions due every week

reviews.content: Didn't love this course. Very useful skillset but I didn't feel supported, had to largely teach myself, and he was quite rude and snarky toward me until I got over the learning curve by myself and started getting questions right. It seems very counterintuitive to punish students for asking questions and make them feel stupid, and only get nicer to them once they already know the answers :/
reviews.workload:
Assignments: 1/week, coding problem set. Spent hours per week on it when I was less confident with coding, less after I got over the learning curve. He only takes up about half the scheduled class time on lecture, the rest is for you to work on the HW and/or leave early.
Final project is the same length but self directed.

reviews.content: This class is also called R for Scientists. He's a good professor, very understanding, and this is a great class is you work in a lab. This class is kind of designed for people doing research and he gives very good practical examples and tailors the class for that.
reviews.workload: There is 1 coding assignment a week with about 20 problems. He's a very fair grader. I think the amount of time the homework will take depends on your skill coding. I am a terrible programmer so it might take me 5-6 hours in total but he gives like an hour in class to work on the assignments.

reviews.content: Professor Callahan is clearly super knowledgeable and enthusiastic about plants and definitely makes an effort to incorporate different teaching techniques through the semester (ie greenhouse trips etc.) However, she can also be a bit disorganized both in her lecture stye and in life. It can sometimes be challenging to follow her lectures and know what material you're responsible for and what is anecdote. This class (at least Fall 2022) was also a 3 hour lecture and by the end of it I could not pay attention. I definitely walked away understanding a lot more about plants and appreciating evolutionary biology but class could be a struggle. Take this if you want to learn more about plants, just bring a coffee beforehand.
reviews.workload: group paper presentation, short response posts for paper presentations (4/semester), 3 homework sets (took maybe 30-45 mins, very chill), midterm and final (her questions can get complex but she is a generous grader)

reviews.content: Lectures themselves were boring. Didn't pay attention at all in class. Powerpoints are a bunch of images and super convoluted figures that are horrible to go back to when studying. Prof. Callahan is such a kind person though. Love the professor, disliked the content but I may just hate plant bio in general.
reviews.workload: Very little workload prob 30mins per week tops. Exams are tough bc it's very confusing but you get a cheat sheet and Prof. Callahan curves.

BUEC B5960.courseName: Banking & Monetary Policy in the Global Economy

reviews.content: I enjoyed the teaching style. Worksheets given allowed me to follow what was happening in class and locate important information later. She did all lectures on the chalkboard and drew out a lot of images. While orgo is a complicated subject, she was really passionate and a very good explainer.
reviews.workload: Achieve homework assignments for every class period (about 10 questions, took between 10-30 minutes) but only the top 20/36 were graded. 3 midterms, but you can drop the lowest grade (all very challenging, try to save your last test to be dropped because it is the most challenging). Weekly problem sets with groups randomly selected to submit, but graded leniently -- you don't have to do them really if you don't want to but they definitely help with understanding material for the exams. reviews.content:
Professor Rojas makes Orgo a fun and engaging class! He's incredibly clear in his explanations, funny, and a really good teacher. He assigns a write up for every class explaining the concepts and then sometimes has a video and usually a set of 2-5 problems to work through. He's been teaching this course forever, but still seems excited and enthusiastic for every class (and not jaded by teaching introductory material.) Class time was a lot of working though problems, with him explaining things. I took this because it was a major requirement and was a little scared because,... orgo, but it wound up being one of my favorite classes! 

If you need to take orgo, do it with Rojas!
reviews.workload:

Very quick and fair grader.

reviews.content:
I can't say enough good things about Professor Rojas!!! I think after teaching the course for so many years, he has it down to a science (no pun intended). He posts an assignment on courseworks each day (so five per week) and holds office hours every single day. The assignments are never due, but if you keep up with them you're good to go for the exams. During the second half of the semester I generally did the assignments every weekend or every other weekend rather than after each class, but it still worked out well. Because Professor Rojas is such a good lecturer that I never felt lost or like I had to teach the concepts to myself, which seems to be pretty rare for intro science classes. I simply showed up to class, did the assignments as much as possible, and learned organic chemistry! I never felt like I was blindly memorizing things or teaching myself from a textbook.

A tip for the last part of the semester - you should keep a running list of new reactions that you learn and organize them by product. Then, memorize the mechanism and the reagents. Having a consistent study group throughout the semester is also helpful! 

Apart from that, Professor Rojas is a really funny guy overall. He reads poetry during class and seems to have a good sense of the pulse of the class (and Barnard in general). If you have to take organic chemistry, you should hands down take it with Rojas.
reviews.workload: 3 midterms and a final. Although it's technically cumulative, the final is heavily focused on material from the last quarter of the class.

reviews.content:
Rojas is the best professor I have ever had. I was really, really struggling the first half of the semester and I went to him asking if I should withdraw, basically freaking out. He was so nice, and empathetic and urged me not to withdraw because I wasn't at that point. He gave me study tips and urged me to come to office hours at least once a week. I highly recommend that if you take this course you go to office hours MORE than once a week. He holds them every day at different times so you should be able to go to at least one. I went every day. These office hours gave me As on the 3 exams after the first 2. He explains and explains and explains like crazy and will answer anything at all. No question is dumb in this class and he takes every question very seriously and makes sure you understand what you need help on. He is so extremely supportive and helpful. His in class notes are also amazing and color coordinated and organized. I have never had any professor so dedicated and so patient. Orgo sucks but I ended up enjoying it a lot more because of him.  
Rojas also got the Emily Gregory Professor Award at Barnard, well deserved.
reviews.workload: 4 midterms (increasing in weight towards grade) and 1 final. daily practice problems for our own use, never turned in (definitely do these if you want an A).

reviews.content:
Professor Rojas is part approachable student-oriented professor, part rock star.

Not an actual rock star like Macklovitch.  But Rojas definitely gave off a rock star vibe in lecture.  He did things like recite Scottish poetry.  He has a good sense of humor.

On the approachable student-oriented side of things, Rojas explains things so clearly, with neat handwriting and color-coding.  He learned most students' names in a lecture course of over 100.  If you don't understand something, and you ask about it in office hours, he will find a way to make you understand.  His flexibility and skill teaching are truly amazing. 

You will love him, and you will love orgo.  In order to also love your orgo grades, my advice is go to office hours at least once a week, preferably more.  Also keep up with the assignments.  Spend at least 15 minutes trying to solve a problem on your own before checking a solution.  If you still don't understand a problem after seeing the solution, ask about it at office hours.  The goal is not just to complete the assignments but to fully understand them.
reviews.workload: Rojas recommends an hour per day, six days per week.  I spent maybe an hour and a half per day, five days per week, and came out with an A.  I never found the orgo lecture course very stressful.  If you keep up, it's perfectly manageable.

I really enjoyed going through the book in this class. I enjoyed the sections that covered key places in China, the section on the minority groups in China, and the simulation of being interviewed for a job. I found those sections both interesting and useful. I have a lot of good memories of the class. I enjoyed listening to my classmates' perspectives. I really enjoyed when Professor Meng shared her perspectives, insights, and experiences (how students have changed throughout her years of teaching, the double standard between empresses and emperors, an image of a dragon circling a pillar in Taiwan). Professor Meng is a teacher who's diligent (often grading/looking over HW after hours and leaving thorough comments), very receptive to feedback, and works very hard in ensuring that all her students are comfortable and bonding (shared lunch and potluck). We went through a Chinese textbook (that she co-authored), and I remember enjoying almost every section with the exception of the dating section/dating show/marriage/passive aggressive in-law sections. I would have preferred a longer section or more time on exploring more of China or Taiwan (especially) of (thinking more practically job-wise, more material centering on navigating China or Taiwan's industries).

The daily quizzes on writing and the readings really did help level up my Chinese in both reading and writing. 

I liked that the daily quizzing forced us to really recollect and recall the characters and I appreciate that the phrases were pulled from/related to the readings. It serves to make them more memorable and a lot more enjoyable than just cold recalling with flashcards (what I've done to self study).

reviews.content:
Xu LaoShi is by far one of the best teachers I've ever had. She comes to every class very enthusiastic and passionate about the material and makes a big effort to give every student attention. 

She truly cares about her students and will go out of her way to make sure we actually understand the material. She is also extremely accommodating and understanding to individual situations, I've had times where I needed to submit a homework late, or times where I wanted to take quizes on other days and she always tries her best to accommodate. 

Learning a language is always a hard process and takes confidence to get things wrong. Xu Lao Shi truly understands this and gives you every opportunity to make mistakes and learn, and encourages students to try things out and learn for themselves. She also ties in real world examples, and makes classes fun by introducing interesting concepts related to the material. She's also extremely knowledgeable about Chinese culture, and youth culture and loves to share little bits of information throughout the classes.

This really helps in creating a sense of community in the classroom and I've made many friends in the class because of this as well. 

I originally took chinese as a language requirement and almost resented Columbia for having this requirement, but with her as a teacher, Chinese is genuinely one of my favorite classes. I'm even considering taking more courses in Chinese just because of this great experience I've had.

Overall I would definitely recommend her as a teacher and her class.

reviews.content: The course itself isn’t too challenging, but the lectures themselves were pretty boring. Blaer goes off topic A LOT (stories about himself that aren’t relevant to the course), doesn’t start talking about content until about 10-15 minutes into the class, and then we “run out of time” at the end. We were behind on content, meaning the last few lectures felt extremely rushed. We actually ended up not learning some things that were stated on the syllabus. In Intro to Java, he actually coded during class, which was very helpful. But then in Data Structures, he stopped coding in front of the class and instead started showing code and essentially read it to us with some explanation. Other times, he pulled up the PDF of the textbook on the big screen and read it off. Not helpful. He writes using paper/sharpie in class, so there are no slides or posted class materials. This meant reviewing before the exams was a pain, since if you didn’t catch something in your notes, you would have to rewatch the lectures (all lectures are recorded) and fast forward the parts where he talks about himself. Also, something that bugged me was that he always says “Homework is gonna come out tonight,” and it almost never came out the same night, always the next day or in two days. He also said our midterm 2 grades would be out “by tonight or tomorrow” multiple times, but it was delayed over 1.5 weeks. Overall, content-wise, the class isn’t bad, and you get ample time for homeworks. However, I did not enjoy my experience in this class. For Intro to Java, you have to purchase a subscription to ZyBooks, which was annoying. I was glad that we did not have to for Data Structures. I will say that Ed Discussion was probably my favorite resource for this class, since the TAs are SO responsive and give great answers.

reviews.content: If you've taken COMS1004 before (or know Java) the transition into this class will be much easier than if you don't, so absolutely make sure you have some understanding of Java. That being said, Blaer's class is good as it doesn't make Data Structures any harder than it needs to be; it's certainly not a weeder class.  Much like his Intro to Java class, attendance is optional and everything you need is posted online or is explained in depth the textbook, you can effectively treat this like an online class with three in person exams. However be warned that this fact does not make Data Structures as a subject any easier, and most people stumble by not taking the class as seriously as they need to. Attend/watch lectures live and ask pointed questions (or engage with Blaers questions). As while Blaer is a decent lecturer you'll find more value in what he has to say if you probe him for a bit more information. Make honest initial attempts on the homeworks despite their length, and clarify things with the TA's (the ones that are nice). The textbook is accessible online, and while you wont need it half the time if you watch lecture, I recommend using it to bolster your understanding as Blaer begins to blitz through certain topics after the first midterm and complete. This is a very manageable class which will reward you if you put the time in, and compared to the other Data Structure's sections I would say Blaer's is your best choice for the least painful experience. Don't go delaying Data Structures by a semester for Blaer though he's not THAT good.

reviews.content: Yes, the syllabus is huge. No, that does not make the class hard. The professor is one of the kindest I have had at Columbia, especially in the CS department. She truly cares about all of her students and wants all of us to succeed. The class is divided into 3 sections (GOFAI, ML, modern AI systems) with one exam per section. This course covers a lot, so if you're looking for a class that goes over every granular detail, this isn't the one to take. However, I felt the syllabus's generality provides a great basis for further learning. The homework is not hard -- doable in a day or two. The exams are also not bad. They are a bit long, but I finished and saw others finish early. The TAs are not supposed to answer questions during exams, but that is pretty standard for the CS department. People tend to skip class because it's recorded, but I really recommend going, especially if you're struggling with the content. Overall, not bad; it's very possible to get an A.

reviews.content:
Honestly, I really liked Toni's teaching style. She and William are very understanding about how hard this course is, and will be patient in explaining the contents for students. I don't think you can make this course any more exciting, but she was able to get the point across.

One thing, though, is that the psets are absurdly hard in my opinion. It feels like nothing she taught during class -- which isn't recorded btw -- helps on the psets, and for some reason, the TAs always beat around the bush instead of giving a very clear, structured way to answer the questions the way they expect us to. I was confused half the time in the class, and the TAs trying to get the information through to me just didn't work because I was just too confused in the first place. Despite not recording lecture + not always posting lecture notes + suggesting readings that were way too dense, they also banned ChatGPT on the homework. I really struggled in the class, but ended up doing fine because of the generous curve.

My main complaint is the timing of the last assignment and the exam. The last assignment was due on the Sunday before we get back from Thanksgiving break, and most of the office hours were either in-person or non-existent, so students weren't able to get a lot of help before the tight deadline. And the final exam was scheduled 3-4 days after we got back from break, leaving barely any time for preparation.

Another thing is that the class had a "I don't know" policy implemented on exams and hws (if you write IDK on a question, you get 20% of the points). Sounds amazing, but a lot of students who tried and showed effort on questions (despite going in the right direction but not getting to a right answer) got lower scores than students who showed no effort and wrote IDK. The policy suddenly changed on the last exam, in which IDK was no longer allowed, and they said they would go back on people's first exam to adjust marks and final grades. That felt pretty messy grading wise to switch up last moment, but probably for the better.

Overall, this course, for me as someone who had never had exposure to the material, pretty much demanded my full attention and work. I think I'd spend 10-12 hours on the last few psets, 15+ hours for the last one because there were few office hours available, so it was very hard for me.

reviews.content: This class is probably GE for most cs majors and my hopes going in is just to finish off with an A and be done with it. The course itself is very proof-based and theoretical. Professor Malkin explains everything clearly and puts in a lot of effort in showing the background behind certain ideas, as well as demonstrating why certain intuitive assumptions do not work. Her notes are also the clearest and easiest to follow I've seen in a long time, and she takes time to review everything important that was learned in the last lecture. reviews.content:

reviews.content:

Everything in this course (assignments, midterm, final) was extremely reasonable in terms of difficulty and workload. You might need to spend some extra time solving the assignments, but it is worth doing because the difficulty of exams closely mirrors the assignments. reviews.content:
Reading other reviews of this class left me surprised, though I believe that Professor Smith took efforts to address student feedback in order to improve class.

That being said, if you are taking this class because you have heard it is easy, Professor Smith is kind Professor, or it just hits a requirement, FIND ANOTHER CLASS. This class is at its best when you actually care about building something for real User Experiences. This also requires a significant effort to engage with the users you state you will serve in your project. Professor Smith IS kind and IS a great Professor who clearly cares about what he teaches. If you just want to have an easy coast class, please spare the seat for someone who actually wants to learn this material. There is so much you can learn from this class and a lot you can actually accomplish in the semester if you figure out something you have passionate for and want to design around. 

You will learn about the psychology around User-Centered Design as well as ways this is actually implemented in industry, while also learning about topics like accessibility, the design cycle, and the absolute importance of grounding your design work in human experience. Of course you will do some front-end work in React and learn about CSS but this is really all in service of learning what it means to design good human experiences with technology.

reviews.content:
Professor Chilton's lectures are extremely engaging.
This class is easy (speaking from someone who doesn't have prior web dev experience). There are only assignments and projects, no exams. Assignments 1-6 helps you practice the web dev stuff you learn in class (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Bootstrap, JQuery, Flask). The Midterm project, which is an individual project, builds on to Assignment 6 (a database website with the topic of your choice) by adding more features and also focusing on graphic design. The Final project, which is encouraged to be done in groups (you choose your own groups as long as your group members are in your TA session, and you can make an exception with your TA to work on it individually), allows you to create a website teaching users a topic of your choice. 
Professor Chilton highly encourages students to use ChatGPT in their assignments and projects, which made this class easy. However, I would encourage you to still engage with the learning process to really benefit from this class. Even if ChatGPT doesn't help, there are 32 TAs holding OHs every week. Note that Professor Chilton does not give out any A+s.
Unlike HWs 1-6 and the projects, some parts in HWs 7-12, which were used to guide students in their final projects, felt like busy work, but I found many parts of them to be very helpful because you can create your prototype and your TA will give you feedback on it. Also, HW instructions often had typos, and I feel like sometimes in the lectures after Spring Break, Professor Chilton repeats the same topics.
Some HWs focused on website functionality, while others focused on both website functionality and graphic design. 
If you want to explore web dev (both the coding and graphic design aspects of it), check out this class!
reviews.workload:
12 (almost) weekly assignments (each counted for 5% of final grade), a Midterm project (10% of final grade), Final project (20% of final grade), participation and attendance in TA sessions after Spring Break (10% of final grade). Lecture attendance is not required, and Professor Chilton posts lecture recordings.
If you follow all the instructions in the HWs and projects and asked for feedback on your work, you will get a 100%. No A+ grades are given out.
BTW: TA sessions are basically these meetings you have with ~10 students and your TA (chosen by you if there's room in the session) each Wednesday after Spring break. Each group talks about their progress on their project/their work in HWs 7-12 and gets feedback from the TA. Before Spring break, lectures were on Mondays and Wednesdays. After Spring break, lectures were only on Mondays, with TA sessions (only 45 mins) being on Wednesdays.

If you're hoping to learn SQL and how to use databases, this class does that... but only for the first few weeks. After that, it is all database management systems, but after the class you do have a pretty good idea of how databases are implemented which is useless for most people at the face level, but very useful for actually using databases. 

Still, the material is boring. Ross lectures as if he understands this fact and has surrendered to his powerlessness in changing it. Every lecture consists of a new topic which he explains well and a few examples. The review lectures are pretty useful. 

Basically, the structure, workload, and instruction of the class are all pretty good thanks to Ross, but you will be falling asleep anyway which is mostly the material's fault.
